content_units: Texas Freelancer Setup Snapshot

For a Texas freelance graphic designer with about   $70,000/year revenue  , home-based operations, and a priority on   simple admin plus some liability protection  , the practical trade-off is straightforward:
-   Sole proprietorship   = simplest and cheapest to start
-   Single-member LLC   = more admin, but better   personal liability separation
-   Taxes are usually very similar by default   for both, unless you later elect S-corp taxation
Situation fit

Because you want   simple admin with some liability protection  , a   single-member LLC is usually the better fit   if you are comfortable with modest setup and maintenance steps. A sole proprietorship is easier, but it does   not   create a legal shield between business risks and personal assets.
Sole Proprietorship vs Texas Single-Member LLC
Topic   Sole Proprietorship   Single-Member LLC (Texas)
Legal status   No separate legal entity; you and the business are the same   Separate legal entity under Texas law
Liability protection   Very limited; personal assets can be exposed to business claims/debts   Better liability separation if you maintain business formalities properly
Startup paperwork   Very low; usually just local/industry registrations and DBA if using a brand name   Must file Certificate of Formation with Texas SOS and create operating docs
Texas formation cost   Usually minimal unless filing assumed name   State filing fee for LLC formation applies
Federal tax treatment   Report business on Schedule C   Default is usually also Schedule C for a single-member LLC
Self-employment tax   Yes, on net earnings   Yes, on net earnings by default
Texas state income tax   None   None
Franchise tax / state filings   No entity-level annual filing like LLC   Texas franchise tax filing/report obligations generally apply, even if no tax is due
Business name protection   Weak unless separately registered/trademarked   LLC name registered with the state, stronger entity-name protection
Banking / separation   Can use dedicated business account, but legal separation is weaker   Strongly recommended to keep separate bank/accounting records to preserve liability shield
Admin burden   Lowest   Low-to-moderate
Best for your priorities   Best for simplicity only   Best balance of simplicity + liability protection
Taxes, Paperwork, and Ongoing Compliance
Tax treatment at your income level
At   $70,000 annual revenue  , your actual tax bill depends on   net profit  , not gross revenue. For a freelance graphic designer, the key tax points are:
-   Federal income tax   applies to profits after deductions
-   Self-employment tax   generally applies in both setups by default
-   Texas has no personal state income tax
- A default single-member LLC is usually a   disregarded entity   for federal tax purposes, so you typically still file like a sole proprietor
Likely deductible expenses
- Home office, if you qualify
- Design software subscriptions
- Computer, monitor, tablet, camera, printer
- Internet and phone business-use portion
- Marketing, website, domain, portfolio hosting
- Contractor payments
- Education directly related to your business
- Mileage or business travel, if applicable
Paperwork differences
Sole proprietorship
- Start working under your own legal name with very little setup
- File a   DBA/assumed name   if using a studio brand instead of your personal name
- Get an   EIN   if you want one for banking/forms or if required for hiring
Single-member LLC
- File formation paperwork with Texas
- Appoint a registered agent
- Create an operating agreement, even if single-owner
- Get an EIN
- Open a separate business bank account
- Use the LLC name consistently in contracts/invoices
Ongoing compliance differences
Sole proprietorship
- Track income/expenses
- Make estimated tax payments if needed
- Renew any local licenses/DBA filings if applicable
- Keep clean records
Single-member LLC
- Everything above, plus:
- File required Texas annual franchise-tax/public-information related filings
- Maintain separation between personal and business finances
- Sign contracts in the LLC’s name
- Keep core company records current
Best Choice for a Home-Based Graphic Designer
Recommended path
Best overall:     Texas single-member LLC
Why it matches your priorities:
- Gives you   some liability protection
- Still keeps taxes relatively simple by default
- Works well for freelancers using contracts, client deliverables, and home-office operations
- Looks a bit more formal to some clients
Trade-off alternative
Best ultra-simple path:     Sole proprietorship
Choose this only if:
- You want the absolute lowest admin burden
- You are comfortable with weaker liability protection
- You may convert to an LLC later once client volume or risk increases
Decision Checklist for 2026
Option 1:   Choose a sole proprietorship     Best if you want the fewest steps and lowest admin burden   Lowest complexity
IRS basics
Option 2:   Choose a Texas single-member LLC     Best if you want simple operations plus a legal liability layer   Stronger legal separation
Texas LLC filing
Option 3:   Use this practical rule     If you sign client contracts, want a business brand, or worry about disputes, lean LLC   Better fit for protection-minded freelancers
Texas taxes
Fast decision test
- Pick   sole proprietorship   if all are true:
- You want the easiest possible startup
- You are okay operating under your own name or simple DBA
- You accept personal liability exposure
- Pick   single-member LLC   if all or most are true:
- You want   some liability protection
- You use client agreements and deliverables
- You want cleaner business separation
- You are okay with formation filing and annual state compliance
Quick Actions
Form an LLC
Get EIN
